speechtext:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving that you do now leave the chaiT for the purpose of enabling the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means, to make good the supply to be granted to His Majesty for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1933, may I at the outset crave your indulgence for those imperfections which are bound to appear in the discharge of a difficult and onerous task on the part of one who has been Minister of Finance for but a few short crowded weeks.
These imperfections will be the more apparent and my task the more difficult when viewed in the light of the brilliant achievements of my immediate predecessor in office.
This review of the year's financial operations will be made under five headings:
(1)	A brief reference to events which have so profoundly disturbed international finance and the consequent reactions on our own situation;
(2)	The financial operations and accounts of the dominion for the fiscal year ended March 31, and in this regard it will be understood that the figures are not final but represent the closest estimates that can be made;
(3)	Canada's trade and commerce;
(4)	The estimated revenue and expenditure for the fiscal year 1932-33, and
(5)	Ways and means for securing the revenues required to meet, the estimated expenditures.

The Budget-Mr. Rhodes
The past year was replete with financial difficulties and problems, many without precedent. Canada, in common with other nations, was in the midst of a period of declining prices and diminishing revenues. During the summer, coming events began to cast their shadow over international finance. The crisis in Germany, following quickly after the collapse in May of the most important bank in Austria, brought sharply to the attention of the world the need for international action upon the vexed question of reparations and inter-governmental war debts. The proposals of President Hoover for a one year moratorium were heralded as a signal for returning world confidence, but the optimism was unfortunately short lived. Although the debt holiday was accepted after some delay, its effect was partially lost in the controversy which served only to emphasize the difficulties of the situation. Meanwhile, the climax drew near, brought on by a repatriation of credits and consequent withdrawals of gold from countries whose reserves had already been reduced. Throughout the world, gold was ceasing to be a medium of exchange, becoming instead a commodity to be jealously guarded. The pound sterling became daily subject to test and finally the world was startled by the announcement on September 21 that Great Britain had been forced off the gold standard. She was followed in rapid succession by many other countries. In the United States, problems arose as a result, on the one hand, of hoarding by individuals, and, on the other, of the effort of their great financial institutions to build up their "liquid position." The fall of foreign exchanges and the dumping of securities brought on practically a demoralization of the investment markets.
It goes without saying that these events had a peculiar significance for Canada, a debtor country, having at the moment an unfavourable trade balance. Our exchange could be maintained only so long as financial operations, based upon normal conditions and confidence, were resulting in a net inflow of money. Between October 1, 1931, and March 31, 1932, the dominion, provinces, municipalities and semi-public bodies, had, it was estimated, S72,000,000 of debt maturing in New York or London, and, in addition, $80,000,000 of external interest charges had to be provided. Added to these, there were the debts of corporations and individuals. With these obligations to be met, the dislocation of external money markets presented no inconsiderable threat to our credit abroad.
Steps had been taken on September 8 to improve our position in New York by the opening up of negotiations for the sale of
$50,000,000 dominion guaranteed bonds of the Canadian National Railways which at that time had $37,000,000 of short-term credits borrowed in that market. The best tender wa.s from a syndicate which purchased $25,000,000 outright and took an option on the remainder. The issue was popularly priced, and the option was exercised. However, much of the buying was on Canadian account, and it was necessary to arrange for partial settlement in Canada, the consequence being that to avoid a serious disruption of the already sensitive exchange situation, only part of the New York short-term loans could be paid off, leaving $18,500,000 to be renewed.
Following the decline in sterling, the Canadian dollar showed -continual depreciation. The low was reached on December 16, when the premium on New York funds was 24J per cent. It was realized that, notwithstanding the high credit position of Canada, any effort to stabilize exchange at par with gold could not, under conditions then existing, be successful. Out policy was therefore directed to accomplishing two results: First, to ensure the prompt payment of all obligations due abroad according to contract and, second, to assist in maintaining normal currency and credit conditions within Canada.
On the 14th of September, the government commenced buying the gold production of the larger Canadian mines, on a basis approximate to the value of New York funds. This gold has been used to meet obligations in New York and has been sufficient to keep the dominion out of the exchange market, and at times to provide external gold funds for the National Railways and provinces. From the viewpoint of Canadian commerce, the policy was generally advantageous.
With respect to the internal situation, the needs of industry, of crop-marketing agencies and of public bodies harassed by falling revenues, made it obligatory that credit facilities in Canada continue to operate smoothly and at reasonable cost to borrowers. Also it was imperative that there be no flight from the Canadian dollar through fear of inflation. This could be accomplished only by maintaining domestic confidence and by preserving a reservoir of credit which could be drawn upon to meet any external crisis. It was successfully accomplished under a policy authorized by the order in council of October 19, which, while maintaining the redemption rights under the Dominion Notes Act, permitted the export of gold only under licence issuable by the Minister of Finance to chartered banks. On the 19th of October, the note issue, including those issued under
The Budget-Mr. Rhodes

the Finance Act, was $144,468,571, and the gold holding represented over 45 per cent of the face value of the issue. On the 19th of March, 1932, the note issue, including those issued under the Finance Act, was $142,896,193; the gold holding,represented over 45 per cent
The number of licences issued to March 1 was 182, representing gold to the value of $28,969,566. Of this amount $19,839,286 was on the Dominion's account, being gold purchased from the mines; the balance was the property of miners, banks and individuals who deal in gold.
Well may Canadians look back with satisfaction over what has been accomplished. All external debts have been met on the due dates. The $72,000,000 principal amount of external debts, payable by the public! bodies of Canada and maturing before March 31, was provided for partly by repayment and partly by renewal, but at this date only $33,000,000 of the original amount is represented by debt owing abroad, and this balance is so arranged that orderly redemption can be carried out without embarrassment. The holders of Canadian securities with obligations for external payment have received their 80 millions of interest as it became due.
This accomplishment, together with the strength of our banking system and stability
of our financial institutions generally, has contributed greatly to the return of confidence, as exhibited in the improvement of the Canadian dollar in the exchange market, and in the higher quotations for Canadian public securities.
Revenues 1931-32
The financial statements published from month to month during the year have indicated that, in common with ail other countries in the world, we have experienced a marked decline in taxation revenue, which represents approximately 83 per cent of the total receipts of the government. Of the major sources, the income tax alone has brought in approximately the sum estimated, having, yielded $61,000,000. Customs receipts fell to $102,800,000, reflecting the drop in the value of imports occasioned by a number of factors, such as the further decline in prices, the unfavourable exchange rate as regards importations from the United States and generally the policy of encouraging production in Canada.
The total receipts from taxes will be $273,300,000, a statement of which, together with the comparative figures for the previous four years, is now submitted.

A major operation for the year was the flotation of the 5 per cent National Service Loan in November. The subscription lists were opened on November 23rd with provision that they might remain open until December 12th. The bonds were offered for public subscription in two maturities at a price of 99-25 and accrued interest for the five-year bonds, and at 99 and accrued interest for the ten-year bonds maturing in 1941. Canadian National Railway Company
The annual report of the Canadian National Railway Company for the year 1931 having already been presented to the house and the whole railway problem being under review by a royal commission, remarks under this head will be confined to a brief statement of the operating results and capital requirements in the year and the financing arranged.

Wheat Marketing Guarantees
Under the authority of section 3 of chapter 58, statutes of 1931, orders in council concerning the marketing of the western grain crops were made. The house will recall the problems which the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, faced in financing its operations in connection with the 1930 crop. The government, believing that it was in the national interest to protect the credit of the marketing agencies in such a way that the grain might be marketed to the general advantage of growers, had given an undertaking to the seven chartered banks concerned, which then made available the necessary credits. The undertaking was given status by order in council P.C. 2238, dated September 12, 1931. This undertaking has served its purpose, and without cost to the treasury. Based upon present market prices, the expectation is that, when all accounts are settled, the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, will be able to settle all advances without recourse being had to the dominion's guarantee.
With respect to the 1931 crop, the three semi-public marketing agencies in the prairie provinces found their position a perilous one at the commencement of the marketing season. The assets usually pledged against bank credits were already encumbered, thus restricting the credit available. Representations on their behalf were made to the Dominion

The ordinary requirements for government services in 1932-33, as provided for in the main estimates, together with certain special and statutory amounts such as for old age pensions and payments to railways under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, are estimated at §369,900,000 and, in addition, $9,600,000 is voted for capital expenditures.
A very considerable contribution to the balancing of the budget has already been made in the reductions of appropriations which have been recommended to the house for the current year. Leaving aside the extraordinary expenditures on wheat bonus and unemployment relief, the expenditures in the fiscal year just ended are estimated at $404,900,000. in comparison with which the estimated expenditures of $379,500,000 for 1932-33 show a reduction of $25,400,000, after absorbing an increase in interest on the public debt of $12,700,000.
The perplexities which ordinarily attend the curtailment of expenditures on governmental services are rendered much greater in the present instance by reason of the reductions which had already been effected in the ordinary and capital expenditures, and particularly by reason of the increasingly smaller proportion of the expenditures which are controllable. Thus in the proposed expenditures for 1932-33, the fixed and, in general, uncontrollable amounts, including debt charges, pensions and ex-soldiers' welfare, provincial subsidies, and similar items, aggregate approximately $236,000,000, leaving only $143,500,000, or 38 per cent, under the classification of controllable. In the fiscal year just ended, the corresponding figure of controllable expenditures was $179,300,000. It will therefore be seen that the reduction which it is proposed to effect this year in the controllable expenditures is $35,800,000, which is the equivalent of 20 per cent. These figures have been cited to illustrate the drastic economies which the government has felt it necessary to institute, having regard to the depleted returns from taxation.
With revenues estimated at $319,100,000 and the usual current expenses of government amounting to $369,900,000, it is clear that increases in the rates of taxation are necessary. Accordingly it is proposed to recommend measures which will, it is estimated, increase the revenues by $55,000,000, thus balancing the current expenditures and leaving a surplus of $4,300,000. If expectations are realized, this surplus would serve to cover a large part of the capital expenditures as well. Even a

slight improvement in price levels, and the general volume of business would, of course, be reflected immediately in the returns from customs and excise taxes, and our budget position would be correspondingly improved.
Without building too greatly on help from this source in the present year, it is the considered view of the government that reductions in expenditures, on the one hand, and proposed additions to the taxation revenues on the other, will, in the final outcome, represent a complete balancing of the budget on the usual current governmental services. While, unfortunately, the estimates of revenues, which are conservatively based having regard to the present conditions of business, do not cover the special expenditures on unemployment relief, nor the more indirect liabilities arising out of the financing of the Canadian National Railways, it is nevertheless, in our judgment, as substantial a step in the direction of providing currently for every responsibility of the government as would be in the public interest to make effective in any one year under existing conditions.
Income Tax
It is proposed to raise the rate of taxation on incomes of corporations and joint stock companies to 11 per cent, to take effect in the 1931 taxation period. Under the act at present, a corporation whose financial year is not coincident with the calendar year is allowed until April 30 of the following year to pay the tax. It is proposed to amend the act to provide in such cases for the return of income and payment of the tax within four months from the close of the fiscal period. This will have the effect of accelerating the collection of the tax from those corporations whose fiscal periods do not end with the calendar year. A further amendment to the Income War Tax Act will repeal the provisions relating to family corporations.
In respect of the tax on personal incomes, it is proposed to repeal the deduction of 20 per cent now allowed from the tax payable under the established schedule of rates. In addition, all taxpayers, including corporations, in receipt of net income in excess of $5,000 will be required to pay a surcharge of 5 per cent of the amount of tax otherwise payable.
The personal exemption, where heretofore $3,000, will be reduced to $2,400, and where heretofore $1,500, will be reduced to $1,200. No change is to be made in the exemption for dependent children. Hereafter the exemption granted in respect of income from annuity

The sales tax will be increased by 2 per cent. Some additional revenue will also be derived from a limited adjustment of the exempt and partially exempt list, in the case of a number of articles not primary products which it is believed should, under present conditions, carry a proportionate share of the tax burden. The special excise tax on goods imported into Canada will be increased by 2 per cent, making it 3 per cent.
Insurance Tax
The tax upon insurance premiums passed at the last session was not put into effect by proclamation as provided by the statute, owing to difficulties over the jurisdiction of the Dominion and provinces in the matter of insurance. It is now proposed, under the Special War Revenue Act, to impose a tax of 1 per cent of net premiums of insurance companies authorized to transact business in Canada or in any province of Canada, other than life, marine and farm mutual. This tax was in force from 1915 to 1929. British and foreign companies, not so authorized but maintaining deposits with the Dominion, will also 'be assessed 1 per cent of net premiums received in Canada. Canadian policyholders who in-

The stamp tax on cheques, .promissory notes, money orders, etc., will be increased. The pre-cent rate is two cents for each instrument exceeding 85. The new rate will be three cents over $5 to $100 and on instruments over $100, six cents. The tax of 10 per cent, minimum 25 cents, on sleeping ear tickets and of 10 cents on each parlour car ticket, will be reenacted. The tax on cable and telegraphic messages will also be reenacted, but the rate will now be five cents for each message costing more than fifteen cents, and the measure will be extended to include long distance telephone calls at the same rate.
A minor amendment also is proposed to the Special War Revenue Act in connection with the stock and bond transfer tax. The present exemption for inter-dealer transactions in bonds is to be repealed and a regulation substituted which will ensure the application of the tax in all transactions except where dealers in securities are acting as purchasing agents for clients.
The sales tax changes come into force immediately; the stamp tax on cheques, telegraph and telephone and transportation taxes, it is proposed to put into effect as of May 2.
Tariff
Having in mind the near approach of the meeting of the Imperial Conference, it is deemed undesirable to make any tariff changes touching the British preference. This decision of necessity precludes any major tariff adjustments.
With one exception, no tariff amendments are therefore proposed. The exception relates to repair parts for farm implements, for which the special rates granted to March 31, 1932, will be further extended to March 31, 1933^
In proposing these additional measures of taxation, consideration has been given, on the one hand, to the ability of our people to bear the extra burden, and, on the other, to the absolute necessity of placing our financial house in order.
Bearing fully in mind the fact that, in common with the whole world, we have suffered -while not in equal degree at least in substantial degree -as the result of a depression universal in scope and of unparalleled magnitude; realizing also the anxieties and burdens of the people and the manifold difficulties resulting from the trying period through which we are passing; and appreciating how desirable
(Mr. Rhodes.]
it is that we should endeavour to the fullest
possible extent compatible with the public interest to call for as little further sacrifice as possible;-at the same time we would be recreant to our duty if we failed to face our problems with determination and at whatever sacrifice, fully meet our financial obligations, balance our .budget and preserve our national credit in the eyes of an observant financial world.
This course may result in hardship. It may entail sacrifice. But in the long run it will result in less hardship, and will call for less sacrifice than that which would flow from a policy less courageous.
Furthermore, the preservation of our national credit is an indispensable prerequisite to the return of prosperity.
While the world is close knit to-day in matters of trade and finance as never before in its history-and we cannot expect normal or prosperous conditions apart from the general world trend-nevertheless some one nation, or group of nations, -must assume the leadership and point the way. To that end an opportunity unique in history is afforded to the British nations, whose representatives will assemble in Ottawa at the Imperial Economic Conference in July next.
If the delegates who assemble here meet in an atmosphere charged with determination to approach their deliberations from the viewpoint of mutual advantage, there will result measures which will give a marked stimulus to empire trade.
And while these measures are primarily designed to stimulate trade within the empire, they will release forces and establish currents which may well flow beyond our borders to the eventual benefit of the world at large.
As a final word, may I say that I do not propose to indulge in prophecy. But I do desire to record my firm conviction that we are not far removed from events which will herald the dawn of better days; that those qualities of courage, resourcefulness and thrift which characterized our forebears are not lost to the present generation; that our struggles and difficulties of to-day will serve as a challenge to greater effort on the part of governments and people to the end that Canada will be found in the vanguard of those nations who successfully emerge from the greatest testing time in modern history.

It is obvious of course,
Mr. Chairman, that the government cannot accept that proposal. The reductions in Great Britain were made under the provisions of a statute which I mentioned to the house on another occasion. Within thirty days from October 1 the minister or ministers were charged with the responsibility of carrying into effect changes by way of reductions that might have been thought desirable or necessary in the public interest. The hon. member for Acadia has said those reductions in some instances were ten per cent and in others 20 per cent. Amongst others the judges received the reduction. Subsequently that action was rescinded. Judges are not servants of the crown; they are the buffers which stand between the crown and the people, when occasion arises, for the purpose of administering justice to all parties who may be litigants, and for the purpose of protecting the people from the crown and from one another. That consideration, which has been elementary with respect to the judges since the Act of Settlement has ultimately prevailed.
I am glad to say a considerable number of judges have communicated not only with the Minister of Justice but with myself indicating their desire to make a contribution of ten per cent of their salaries to the public weal. They have asked that appropriate action be taken in that regard. I may say the same thing has occurred with respect to. the others. With respect to lieutenant-governors of the provinces however I should like to point out that they are not in receipt of salaries sufficient to enable them to discharge the duties devolving upon them by reason of their offices. In consequence of that fact it is very difficult to get any person to undertake the duties of that office. The salary is so inadequate as compared with the necessary expenditures that it is not only undesirable to cut their salaries but a compulsory reduction of the salaries of representatives of the crown is not a matter which could be undertaken under present conditions in this parliament, for reasons which I think are fairly obvious.
I do not think I should mention any names, because it would be wholly improper to do so, but I may say that one, lieutenant-governor said he would have to leave his office if the ten per cent cut applied to his salary. Some of them have. taken office at very con-

Mr. Chairman, so far as I
am personally concerned I am opposed to this bill in its entirety. I so expressed myself when the resolution was first before the house, but in view of the fact that a day or two ago
the bill was given second reading, that is, its principle was adopted, I realize that it is useless for me to say very much. However,
I do feel that clause (b) should be amended to leave out all the words after the word "Canada" in the sixth line, as by deleting the remainder of the subsection, "the Governor General of Canada, the lieutenant-governors of the several provinces of Canada, the members of the judiciary, and the members of the military, naval and air forces of Canada, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police," would come within the scope of the bill. I do not think it is in the interest of the country that these civil servants should be exempted from the ten per cent reduction, while members of this house and of the Senate and the civil service generally are forced to relinquish ten per cent of their remuneration.
As I said a moment ago, I am opposed to this bill in its entirety, but since the house has adopted the principle, I submit we should go the whole distance-nobody should foe exempted from the operation of the bill. I cannot agree with what the right hon. gentleman said about exempting lieutenant-governors, judges or anybody else from the ten per cent reduction. When the resolution was first placed on the order paper I remember reading in the public press a statement by His Excellency the Governor General that he was willing to give ten per cent of his salary towards the revenues of Canada. It seems to me that when we are asking elevator men, charwomen and every other civil servant to take a ten per cent reduction in their remuneration, we should not turn down His Excellency's offer. I submit that in view of that offer and in view of other facts, His Excellency should be placed in the same position as members of the Senate and of the House of Commons and everybody else who is covered by this bill.
My right hon. friend told us that the lieutenant-governors were not getting sufficient remuneration. That may be so, but I should like to know which lieutenant-governor did not ask for the position which he now occupies? Which lieutenant-governor would give it up if there was no salary attached to his office? If any lieutenant-governor mentioned by the right hon. gentleman thinks his official salary not sufficient, let him resign, and let the government appoint other men to the office subject to a ten per cent reduction in salary.
Let me go a step further. We have dealt with members of the judiciary. If, as my right hon, friend says, they have written him and other members of the cabinet expressing

My understanding is that no member of the militia force has a contract with the government any more than any other civil servant, that when they join the force they fill out a certain form and sign it, and if my information is correct they agree to take a lower rate of pay if the government should ask them to do so. I want to add my
endorsation of the amendment now before the committee. Since the Prime Minister has stated that the amendment is not acceptable to the government, however, I am afraid there is very little hope that it will be adopted, since the government commands a strong majority in the house.
I am not in the same position as the preceding speaker, who stated that he was opposed to the bill in its entirety. I voted for the ten per cent deduction for several reasons. I realized that there was a serious situation existing throughout the country. We have just listened to the budget presentation by the Minister of Finance, and I am sure we all realize that the balancing of the budget made very necessary economies such as this ten per cent deduction, and since the measure is to apply for one year only I think most of us
can stand that cut of ten per cent. The amount each will contribute will not be very large, and the cost of living has dropped approximately fifteen per cent, so our loss will not be as great as the benefit we will obtain through the decreased cost of living.
I had in mind also the conditions existing in the west. There are thousands of farmers, business men, school teachers and others in western Canada who would be thankful indeed to receive the salary paid the average civil servant in this city, even with the ten per cent reduction. We have public school teachers out there receiving only a few hundred dollars a year, while others are teaching for just a small government grant and boarding around among the people, in order to continue the work.
But, Mr. Chairman, while I favour the bill in general, I do not favour the exemptions outlined in section 2. The Prime Minister has said that he has received letters from some judges stating that they are willing to take the ten per cent cut voluntarily. In fairness to those judges I think the others who have not so volunteered should be required to contribute ten per cent. I am convinced that no hardship will be worked on any judge if the ten per cent reduction is extended to cover their salaries. The salary of the lowest paid judge in Canada is $5,000 from the Dominion treasury, and that amount is supplemented in various provinces; in my own province, for instance, the judges receive $1,500 in addition. I would make bold to say, also, that we are over-judged in this country.

By actual count we
have 286 judges in the Dominion of Canada. I think if we compared our judiciary and the total population of this country with the number of judges and the population of the British Isles, we would feel like hiding our faces because of the extravagance we have exhibited in connection with the salaries of the judges in Canada. That being the case, it offers an added reason why we should insist that every one of the 286 judges in Canada should contribute ten per cent of his salary towards helping to meet the urgent situation now confronting us.
I listened with considerable interest to what the Prime Minister had to say with regard to the lieutenant-governors, but I should like to know why the salary of the High Commissioner for Canada has been reduced from $10,000 to $9,000. An item appearing on page 10 of the estimates shows that a reduction of

ten per cent has been made in the salary of this gentleman, while the salaries of the lieutenant-governors have been left unchanged. It would seem to me that the expenses of this gentleman are just as great as if not greater than those of the lieutenant-governors; if a deduction is fair in the one instance, it would be equally fair in the other.
I cannot see any justification for exempting the members of the military, naval and air forces from the proposed reduction of ten per cent. We have been told that there are 139 persons in the department of National Defence drawing salaries between $4,000 and $4,900, thirty drawing salaries between $5,000 and $5,900 and fifteen drawing salaries between $6,000 and $6,900. A total of 184 persons in that department draw salaries of $4,500 per year or over. A deduction of ten per cent should not cause any hardship to any of these persons.
It is rather difficult to state exactly how much revenue would accrue if this deduction was levied against those at present exempted, but I have made an approximate computation. Judges of Canada draw something over $2,000,000 in salaries, and a ten per cent reduction would amout to about $214,190. If this deduction were applied to the officials of the Department of National Defence, it would mean a saving of over $88,000, and if it were applied still further to the non-permanent active militia and the permanent forces, it would amount to between $600,000 and $800,000. A considerable saving would be made if this deduction were applied to the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, although there is a question as to whether or not there is justification for making the reduction when the salaries are paid by the provinces.
His Excellency the Governor General has made a voluntary offer to accept a ten per cent reduction in his salary, and I think his action deserves the thanks of this chamber. His Excellency is not a Canadian by birth but he has set an example which I think is worthy of the commendation of every hon. member of the house.
If this reduction were applied to the salaries of the lieutenant governors, the judges and the members of the militia and mounted police, there would be an added revenue of over one million dollars. It would be only fair, it would be only equitable, it would be only right that these gentlemen should make a contribution to the finances of this country on a par with that being made by the members of this house and of the Senate.

I shall not inflict upon the committee the argument which has been made so fully in the law journals and to which I made reference the other day, nor shall I refer to the editorial comments made by British papers as to the error of seeking to reduce the salaries of British judges.
With reference to the lieutenant-governors of the provinces, I can only say that the court of last resort in the empire has held that within the boundaries of the provinces these gentlemen represent the sovereign, and to reduce their compensation by this statute would be to act at variance with the long series of precedents which have obtained with respect to matters of this kind. Some hon. members may well say that I have not seemed to be bound by precedents where it is necessary to change them; I admit that quite freely, but I believe it would be wrong to depart from the principle established in this regard. The offer made by His Excellency the Governor General has been accepted by the government; I do not believe the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough was in his place the other evening when I read a statement to this effect.
We come to the third of the three classes, the crown, the judiciaries and the forces of the crown. The men who come within this third class are under discipline-they cannot resign even if they so desire. They are not under an ordinary contract, they are enlisted men, and the government contracts that during the term of their enlistment they shall receive a given compensation. It is not a contract in the ordinary sense because the word "enlistment" is used rather than the word "contract." They cannot leave the service without being guilty of desertion and prosecution, and they cannot resign.

With respect to the third class, the forces of the crown, presumably we have the power to change the terms of the enlistment, but the government is of the opinion that this should not be done.
The action taken by the government in this instance does not arise out of any desire to do other than what is fair to all parties in the state. But there must be a frank recognition by parliament of the fact that the crown, the judiciary and the forces of the crown are in a position different from that occupied by any of the classes covered by the bill. I shall not, as I said, dwell on the first two. As to the third class, if they were occupying a position such as has been suggested, the matter might be looked at from another angle. But from a question of law, apart from any other consideration, the forces of the crown occupy the position I have indicated and there is not an hon. member of this committee who does not understand that enlistment and contract are different. In the latter case, there is freedom to leave the position you have, while in the other, a man cannot leave his position except by becoming a deserter.

It merely beclouds the issue by, shall I say, dragging in such terms as "the crown," which would indicate that there is something sacrosanct about arrangements as they now stand.
Let me refer particularly to the lieutenant-governors. The position taken a few minutes ago by the Prime Minister was that it was exceedingly difficult to get anyone to occupy lieutenant-governorships. speechtext: Coming to realities, we all know that to a very considerable extent to-day this position is, I think I may say, formal and social in character. Whatever the constitutional aspect may be, in practice the duties are very largely formal and social.

The expenses undoubtedly are incurred very largely in social functions. Since that is the real fact of the case, the sooner we reach the point where we shall abolish these lieutenant-governorships altogether, the better for everybody concerned, and that idea is coming rapidly to be felt by large sections of the people in Canada. I know of no better way of hastening this consummation than by carrying such an amendment as the one before us, because by doing so we assist very materially in having a still larger number of people reject these honours. Before very long people will come to understand there will have to be changes in the British North America Act, changes in our relationships, but just because of certain technical matters I do not think we ought to be asked to go on forever supporting institutions of this nature. It seems absurd that the postman who comes to our door and who is already underpaid and that many civil servants who are to-day being turned out on the street because of these cuts, should be made to suffer in this way, while people who are occupying what are essentially formal and social positions go scot-free. speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows the reason for the change. It does away with two series of overheads. That is the whole story.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I know that, but that is another point. We have in Ottawa an overhead whereby at least one official of Royal Canadian Mounted Police is receiving a salary of $12,000 or over. I cannot quite understand why a man who is obtaining a salary of $12,000 or over should be retained in that position and not be subject to the cut to which other people in government employ are subject.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: And he can resign.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Yes, he can resign if he wishes. To revert to the other point, the Prime Minister knows very well that before he came into office there was a good deal of friction between the mounted police in Saskatchewan and the provincial police of that province. The provincial police rather resented the coming into that province of the mounted police. It is very doubtful whether it was necessary for some years to have two distinct police forces there. The Dominion government, however, retained their police force here and now we are told, because there would be a saving of one overhead, we must have a centralized police force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I am sure he desires to be fair. The provinces have asked the dominion to take over the administration of the police and merge the two into one. In no case has this been done at the instance of the federal power; it has been asked by the local or provincial authorities.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I accept that explanation; in fact, I have information to that effect directly from some of the provincial premiers. But that does not alter my argument that the federal government might have withdrawn the mounted police force from, say

Saskatchewan, and allowed that province to carry on, thus saving money to the dominion treasury. The federal authorities did not wish to do that; they wished to retain their police force and keep up this enormous overhead. Under those circumstances the provinces, in order to save money for themselves, consented to give up their own police force, merging it into the larger one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Under the provisions of the Customs and other acts, we have to maintain a preventive force. That work has now been taken over by the mounted police. Therefore there is a further saving so far as that phase of the question is concerned.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I can understand there may be some saving. I do not want at present to go into the other matter which I should like some time to discuss, that is of the danger of a centralized police force. That underlies and I think more than overcomes the economy that may be secured under the recent arrangement. All I am pointing out at this time is that it is an entirely wrong principle that a police force should be exempt when other people equally worthy and doing equally good work in the service of the country should be subjected to a cut of this character. Only yesterday, I think it was, a watchman was laid off and his job taken over by a mounted policeman. Had a watchman been doing the work he would be subject to the ten per cent cut, but to-day a Royal Canadian Mounted Policeman being on the job, the latter is not subject to the cut. The work is practically the same, and with all deference to the Prime Minister's statement with regard to the forces of the crown, I cannot see why men who are safeguarding government property or acting as ornaments in the art gallery or anything of that kind, should not be subject to a cut just as much as any other civil servant.
The same argument applies to the defence forces. The Prime Minister was not very explicit when he referred to British experience.
I presume that he referred to the riots which took place when there was a reduction in the pay of the navy. I hope he does not imply that if the salaries of our militia were reduced there would be riots in this country, but I think that that was his implication. Surely that is not true! It seems to me that since so many of the higher salaries are being paid to those engaged in the national defence, as the hon. member for Kindersley pointed out, and since they may resign if they wish to do so, there is no particular reason why they should be exempted as is proposed. It

Public Service-Salary Deduction
is all very well to talk of having entered upon certain terms of enlistment. But may I point out that many of the civil servants have enlisted in the civil service of this country ten, fifteen or twenty years ago, giving up lucrative employment elsewhere to do so, and giving up the prospect of promotion elsewhere. They entered the civil service of this country on the implicit understanding that their tenure of office would be secure. To-day a good many of them are being let out, and the rest of them have had their salaries cut down below What they would ordinarily receive under the statutory arrangements. It seems to me that this is all wrong, and I join with others who have protested against it in urging that we should have equal treatment for all classes of those who are receiving payment from this country.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Before we leave this question about the judiciary, I am not quite sure whether the judiciary includes the ex-judges as well as the judges. I would ask the government if I am correct in assuming that the judges on pension are not subject to this ten per cent reduction. I notice on pages 22 and 23 of the estimates for 1932-33 a large number of estimable gentlemen who are receiving very large pensions. I will only read the first three names, for instance, on page 22. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick receives a pension ol $6,666.66. I would like to know if his pension is subject to this ten per cent reduction, and if not, why he gets off without making this ten per cent contribution while the Finance Minister and I have to pay it. The same question applies to the next gentleman on the list, who receives a pension of $8,000, and also to the third gentleman, P. B. Mignault, who receives a pension of $12,000 a year. It seems to me that unless the pensions of these gentlemen are subject to this reduction, the act should be amended to include them, for surely a man who is drawing a pension of $12,000 a year and is carrying on a law business in a city of Canada should come under the provisions of this bill just as much as the elevator men and the ligihtkeepers and the charwomen and the members of parliament. Consequently I say that this act should bs amended.
With further regard to my argument as to the blanketing-perhaps I should have said whitewashing-the provincial police into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I observe that in addition to the provincial police the land forces of the preventive service were also taken into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Now if the land forces 41761-H2i	.
of the preventive service had not been taken into the mounted police in the last few days they would have been subjected to this reduction of ten per cent, but because they have been taken into the mounted police the preventive service officers who work upon the land are not subject to the reduction.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: They get less money.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I do not care whether they
get less money or not. The labourer is worthy of his hire, and if they are not getting more pay it is perhaps because they are not worth any more. I am going to argue this like my hon. friend would argue it if he were in court.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
May I congratulate you if
you do?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: My argument is this: Because the land forces of the preventive service are taken from the department of my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue and put into the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice under the guise or under the heading of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, they are not subject to this reduction of ten per cent, while the members of the preventive service who still remain under the Minister of National Revenue and whose work is much more hazardous than that of the land forces-I am referring now to the captains, officers and sailors on the preventive boats on the Atlantic and Pacific-have to suffer the ten per cent reduction. The land forces go scot-free and the members of the far more hazardous branch of the service have to suffer the reduction. I say that that is not fair, and I appeal to the Minister of Justice and to the Minister of Finance to see that the act is amended so that both these branches of the service will be treated alike. I should like an answer to my question, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the judges and ex-judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
The ex-judges are in the
same position with respect to their pensions as the judges with respect to their salaries.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
They do not pay the ten per
cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I would like to say a
word or two with respect to the proposed amendment as it would affect judges in the province of Manitoba. Under date of the first of April there appeared in the Winnipeg Evening Tribune an open letter from Judge Stubbs, of the city of Winnipeg, to the premier of the province of Manitoba, in which he states that he has been informed by the

Public Service-Salary Deduction
premier himself that the government of the province of Manitoba proposed to tax the county court judges of the province in respect to their surrogate court salaries, which I might say are paid by the province. The proposal as set out in Judge Stubbs' letter was that the salary which Judge Stubbs receives for the performance of his surrogate court duties, namely, $2,500, was to be taxed by $1,350, and that the salaries of the other county court judges who receive $1,500 for the performance of their surrogate court duties were to be taxed by $1,000. The county court judges in the province of Manitoba receive a salary of $5,000 from the dominion government, and $1,500 from the provincial government for the performance of their surrogate court duties, with the exception of Judge Stubbs, in Winnipeg, who receives $2,500 in this latter respect. Judge Stubbs, in a spirited letter, wrote to the premier protesting against this tax and pointing out that so far as the province is concerned the tax amounts to fifty per cent of the salary which is paid to these judges by the provincial government. Some two or three days later Mr. Major, the attorney general for the province of Manitoba, replied on behalf of the government, intimating, while not directly saying so, that the tax would be put into effect. If we add to that tax a further reduction of ten per cent on the $5,000 salary which these judges receive from the dominion government, surely it is not treating the county court judges of the province of Manitoba in the manner in which they are entitled to be treated as judges of our courts.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Let them resign, then,
if they are dissatisfied.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
That is a very smart
reply.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: It is a true reply, too.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: You might make the same reply to all the other civil servants whose salaries have been cut.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: The Prime Minister said the civil servants could resign.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: My hon. friend is receiving a ten per cent cut in his indemnity; why does he not resign?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I will resign any time
my hon. friend will.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I suggest that my hon.
friend should not try to make a hero of himself. Quite frankly, I should have liked
to see the judges throughout Canada come forward, as has the Governor General, and submit voluntarily to a ten per cent cut. I

believe they would improve their position in the minds of the public if they were to do that.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Let us improve it for them.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I have in my hand a
letter dated March 7, 1932, from a county court judge in the province of Manitoba, from which I should like to read one or two paragraphs :
I gather from press reports that the matter of a reduction in judges' salaries will be the subject of some debate, or at least remarks or opinions by members of the house, also that the power of the government to reduce such salaries is apparently in some doubt.
In speaking for myself only I have no hesitation in saying that if a voluntary consent by the judges to a reduction would be of assistance to the government, I would be happy to do my part.
If the matter comes up you will know my ideas on the subject, and have my hearty support and cooperation in any way that will help bridge the difficult period we are going through.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Will the hon. member give
the judge's name?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: This letter is from Manitoba. If any hon. member wishes to see the letter he is at perfect liberty to do so. I hope hon. members will agree that I should not give the judge's name.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am stating what I believe
to be the rule. If an hon. member reads a letter he should give the name of the writer. I ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I have read only some
excerpts.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: What is the ruling?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: There are occasions, when a letter is not of a controversial nature, where it is desirable to withhold the name of the writer. I think the house usually agrees that in such cases the names should not be given. There is nothing controversial about the letter which has been read.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
As to
whether or not the letter is judged controversial depends on which side of the house an hon. member may happen to sit.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Not at all.

speechtext:
I had a
similar experience a couple of years ago. Although the letter was of a noncontroversial nature the minister was one of the first to ask for the name of the writer.

speechtext: On this occasion it is from a member of the judiciary. Surely my hon. friend will not insist upon the production of the name, particularly when the hon. member for Dauphin has agreed to show the letter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the
Winnipeg Evening Tribune of April 4, I find an editorial under the heading "Independence of the judiciary." At this point I should like to read one or two paragraphs from the editorial:
There are further facts to be taken into consideration.
Judge Stubbs is not a member of the civil service of the province or of the dominion. He is a judge. The complete independence of the judiciary has long been recognized in English law. Independence, it was decided long ago, can be achieved only by permanence of tenure of office and absolute security in remuneration.
It is a cardinal principle of our judicial system that judges are appointed for life, and can be removed from office only by impeachment proceedings which are so carefully safeguarded that a judge must be very clearly unfitted for his high office before he can be removed from it. He is not subject to removal because of the displeasure of any government, or even of the crown itself.
Along with the assurance of permanence in his appointment must go absolute security of remuneration. That is at least one-half of the guarantee of his independence, because, if his salary is subject to the whims of a government or a political majority, he can obviously have no real independence. The power to reduce or refuse to pay his salary would constitute practically the same control over his acts and judgments as the power to remove him from office altogether.
I have pointed out this anomaly in so far as it exists in the province of Manitoba. I think hon. members will agree that we would be most unfair if we were to ask judges receiving salaries of $7,500 to consent to a reduction of $1,850, or those receiving salaries of $6,500 for a contribution in any one year of $1,500. For those reasons I cannot support the amendment.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Referring to the judges in Manitoba, my hon. friend said they were subject to the tax on their surrogate court salaries. What about the judges in the other provinces?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I am not making any comments in that connection. I have already stated my views.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment. I thought the arguments of the Prime Minister were inconclusive. He has said that the judges are not civil servants, but that they act as buffers between the crown and the common people. I should think that would be true only in cases of litigation in
the exchequer court, and hon. members know that that court performs only a very small part of the judicial activities of the judges. In ordinary court cases one would suppose that judges acted as buffers as between man and man, or between law-abiding portions of the community and those seeking profit by crime. I believe we are entitled to draw an inference from an hon. member's remarks, and especially from the remarks of a member as capable as the Prime Minister of expressing himself. The inference we might draw from his remarks would be that if judges' salaries were reduced their function as buffers would be imperilled or lessened, and that citizens would not be buffered as well as they were before. I do not think any judge would care to lend himself to that view. I think the test is on the question of salary. Do the judges receive salaries which could properly be reduced? When we know that members of parliament are receiving a cut which is equivalent in their case to 30 per cent or more, I do not know why judges receiving $5,000 to $15,000 per year should not be cut to the extent of ten per cent. Several hon. members have said that judges have written saying that they would agree to a cut. I submit that that is the answer to the suggestion that we should not tax them. They themselves recognize that they can afford to pay, and that it is proper they should do so. Is that not the answer to the suggestion that their salaries should not be cut? If it is right to accept a proportion of salary from one judge, or from half a dozen, would it not be better to have the contributions uniform? Otherwise we will have a condition which obtained not long ago in connection with a certain member of a legislature in one of the provinces. He made a gesture by rejecting a certain portion of his salary. After he left office the money was not disturbed, until he took advantage of his undisputed rights and asked for the payment of the moneys lying to his credit. I do not say that would be true in connection with the judges or other people who would voluntarily agree to make a contribution, but there would always be that danger, possibly from heirs of a deceased judge. If it is right to do it for some of the judges, or some of them at least think it so, why not make it apply all round?
As regards the lieutenant-governors, as my friend has said, the office of lieutenant-governor is regarded by many people as a high honour, and wealthy men are always glad to take the position. I do not know what the custom is in the east, but in British Columbia our lieutenant-governor does not

pay income tax-and the income tax is pretty steep out there and is going to be steeper. Possibly the release from income tax would add very considerably to the admittedly small salary that the lieutenant-governor gets in proportion to his expenses. The suggestion has been made that in the case of one man at any rate he would be compelled to resign. Well, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest -and men with more claim to statesmanship than I possess have taken the same view- I would say, let them resign, let us do away with all the lieutenant-governors. I do not apply that to the governor general perhaps, but let us do away with all the lieutenant-governors in this time of financial stress and anxiety. This dominion got along for the greater part of last session without a governor general, and we find that in Ontario they managed to worry along during the recent session without a lieutenant-governor either to open or close the proceedings. No doubt the duty was performed perfectly well by the chief justice of the province. I think it would be a good gesture in these days if we did away with our lieutenant-governors altogether.
As to the army and navy, the Prime Minister in his later remarks pointed out that there was more than a contractual arrangement, that it was a question of enlistment and the rank and file could not resign. That is true. But it could be easily got around by the government making the ten per cent reduction, and if any member of the permanent forces did not approve of it, give him an opportunity to leave the service. So far as making the reduction by " force of arms," so to speak, I do not think that would be right. I speak with some feeling because I was once a victim of something similar at the hands of the ancestors of the government now in power, because it was a Conservative government that cut my pay. I had enlisted with the permanent corps at its certain, agreed wage-a very small one. After some months I was advised that my remuneration had been cut down. Coming from a frugal country that did not strike me as being a fair demand. I put forward the very arguments advised by the Prime Minister to-day, that you cannot enlist a man and then cut down his scale of pay. I went before a board-there were officers galore, the general commanding, colonels, majors and other officers, and I took considerable risk of being put in the guard room for insubordination because I dared to stand on my rights. After a great deal of argument and discussion I was told that I could not get the rate 
of pay for which I had enlisted. But I got around it in another way.
As regards the suggestion that something might happen here if, as in Britain, we should enforce a ten per cent reduction, why was it said if it was not meant? The suggestion was: Look at what happened in Britain in connection with the reduction in the pay of the navy. I do not do anyone any injustice when I say it was found that the men of that particular grade had had their pay cut to an unreasonable extent, and to an extent far greater than the reduction applied to those drawing much higher salaries. There was good ground for the complaint by the men; but after all it was .made in a most orderly way and only as a complaint. If there was not any such implication, why was the point made? The implication there is: "We had better be careful; if we meddle with the pay of the army and navy in Canada some weakness may develop which may imperil our safety.' I do not think that is a pleasant implication, and having been a member of the permanent force, I take it upon myself to say there is no danger of any feeling of that kind being generated even if this cut is put into effect. But if there is any suoh danger, the sooner we find it out the better. If our army and navy are so unreliable that a ten per cent cut in pay for one year in the face of every civil servant in Canada having to take such a reduction, means that weakness will develop, the sooner we find it out the better. But the men of our army and navy have too much loyalty-not in the flag waving sense, but in the real sense of the word-to object to share in a general cut in pay. We have not heard of any letters to the Prime Minister from the rank and file volunteering to contribute ten per cent of their pay, and we do not know whether they have been given a chance to make such offer, but I am sure that no feeling of disloyalty would be engendered by a ten per cent cut-regret of course; but not disloyalty-but if any of them should consider a ten per cent cut improper because they are enlisted men, then give them the opportunity to withdraw from the service. In these days of unemployment I do not think very many would withdraw.
For these and many other reasons, that I cannot now dwell upon, Mr. Chairman, I certainly hope the amendment will pass. The right hon. Prime Minister, said of course he could not accept the amendment. But I do not see any necessity why it should not be accepted in the spirit in which it was put forward by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner).
